developmental_goal: Support healthy development of the baby's brain and spine through folate-rich foods
required_materials: Dark leafy greens, beans and groundnuts
activity_description: Include at least one folate-rich food at every main meal: dark leafy greens, beans, lentils or groundnuts. Plan the week's meals so these foods appear daily, and cook greens lightly so they keep their goodness. Keep taking any folic acid tablets your antenatal clinic gives you, since food alone rarely provides enough.
cultural_relevance: Managu, terere, kunde, sukuma wiki, beans, ndengu and groundnuts are affordable folate-rich foods found in most Kenyan markets.

activity_name: Iron and Folic Acid Tablets with a Daily Routine
developmental_goal: Prevent maternal anaemia and support the baby's growth through daily iron and folic acid supplementation
required_materials: Iron and folic acid tablets from the antenatal clinic; a cup of water
activity_description: Take the iron and folic acid tablets your antenatal clinic provides every day, exactly as the health worker advises. Link them to something you already do daily, such as the evening meal, so you don't forget. Keep them where you will see them but out of children's reach, and tell the health worker if they upset your stomach.
cultural_relevance: Antenatal clinics in Kenya provide iron and folic acid tablets during pregnancy; a family member can help with reminders.

activity_name: Eggs, Milk and Fish for Baby's Brain
developmental_goal: Provide iodine and choline that support the baby's brain development
required_materials: Eggs, milk or yoghurt, small fish
activity_description: Add foods that supply iodine and choline to your week: eggs, milk or yoghurt, and fish. Aim to include one of them in a meal or snack most days. Cook eggs and fish all the way through, and choose pasteurised or boiled milk.
cultural_relevance: Omena, eggs, mala and boiled fresh milk are familiar, affordable sources in many Kenyan homes.

activity_name: Healthy Snacks for the Growing Baby
developmental_goal: Meet the extra energy needs of the second and third trimesters with nutritious snacks
activity_description: From the second trimester your body needs a little more food each day. Instead of sugary snacks, prepare one or two healthy snacks such as fruit, a handful of groundnuts or plain yoghurt. Keep a snack ready to carry when you go out so you don't go long without eating.
cultural_relevance: Bananas, pawpaw, mangoes, oranges, roasted groundnuts and mala are easy, low-cost snacks.

developmental_goal: Protect the growing baby from tobacco smoke and alcohol, which harm development
activity_description: Talk as a household about keeping the home free of tobacco smoke and alcohol during pregnancy and after the baby arrives. Ask anyone who smokes to do so outside and away from the pregnant mother. If someone at home wants to stop smoking or drinking, ask the health worker what support is available.
cultural_relevance: Agreeing on house rules together, including with visitors and older relatives, helps everyone protect the baby.

developmental_goal: Reduce smoke exposure for the mother and the baby by improving cooking ventilation
required_materials: Windows or doors that open; a safer cookstove if available
activity_description: Look at where you cook and how smoke leaves the room. Open windows and doors while cooking, cook outside when you can, and keep the pregnant mother and young children away from smoke. Ask about safer, cleaner cookstoves if smoke often fills the house.
cultural_relevance: Many Kenyan homes cook with firewood or charcoal on a jiko; cooking in a well-ventilated area or outdoors cuts smoke.

activity_name: Calm Music Time in the Third Trimester
developmental_goal: Offer the baby gentle music to hear as their hearing develops before birth
required_materials: A phone or radio with soothing music, or your own humming
activity_description: In the last three months of pregnancy, set aside a few minutes a day to play gentle, soothing music or lullabies while you rest. Keep the volume soft and comfortable. Notice whether the baby moves or settles, and enjoy the calm time for yourself too.
cultural_relevance: Gentle Kenyan lullabies, church hymns or soft instrumental music all work; choose what the family enjoys.

activity_name: Reading a Story to the Bump
developmental_goal: Help the baby begin to recognise caregivers' voices before birth
activity_description: Choose a short story, poem or passage and read it aloud to the baby for a few minutes each day, in a calm voice. Reading the same piece often helps the sounds become familiar. Partners and older children can take turns reading too.
cultural_relevance: Read in Kiswahili, English or the family's mother tongue, whichever you will speak to the baby after birth.

activity_name: Morning and Evening Greetings for the Baby
developmental_goal: Build a daily habit of talking with the baby before birth
activity_description: Start and end each day by greeting the baby: say good morning, tell them what the day holds, and say goodnight before sleep. Place a hand on the bump while you talk if you like. Small, regular conversations help you bond and help the baby learn your voice.
cultural_relevance: Greetings in the family's own language, such as 'Habari ya asubuhi, mtoto', make the habit feel natural.

activity_name: Telling the Baby About Your Day
developmental_goal: Expose the baby to everyday speech and strengthen bonding before birth
activity_description: While you cook, walk or rest, describe what you are doing out loud to the baby: what you are cooking, who you met, what you can see. There is no need to use special words; normal, warm talk is what the baby needs to hear.
cultural_relevance: Works during daily tasks such as fetching water, cooking ugali or going to the market.

developmental_goal: Prepare a set of familiar songs to use from birth, especially at bedtime
activity_description: Pick two or three songs or rhymes the family loves and sing them to the bump regularly. Keep using the same songs after birth, especially as part of the bedtime routine, when a familiar voice and tune can help calm the baby.
cultural_relevance: Traditional lullabies and songs from grandparents can be passed on this way.

activity_name: Talking to the Baby During the Ultrasound
developmental_goal: Notice the unborn baby's responses to caregivers' voices and touch
activity_description: If you have an ultrasound scan, bring your partner or another caregiver. While you watch the screen, talk to the baby and ask the health worker whether you can see the baby respond to your voices or movements. Talk afterwards about what you noticed.
cultural_relevance: Including fathers and grandmothers in clinic visits helps the whole family bond with the baby.

developmental_goal: Keep the pregnant mother physically active with regular moderate activity
activity_description: Unless your health worker has advised otherwise, aim for about 30 minutes of brisk walking on most days, adding up to at least 150 minutes a week. Walk at a pace that raises your breathing but still lets you talk. Drink water, avoid the hottest part of the day, and stop if you feel dizzy or unwell.
cultural_relevance: Walks to the market, church or a neighbour's home can count; walking with a friend makes it easier to keep going.

developmental_goal: Help the mother exercise safely without exhausting herself
activity_description: Use the talk test whenever you exercise: you should be able to hold a conversation while moving. If you can't speak comfortably, slow down. Keep up the activities you already do, ask your health worker which exercises suit your pregnancy, and rest when you need to.
cultural_relevance: Useful for everyday activity such as walking uphill, carrying shopping or doing farm work.

developmental_goal: Ease stiffness and keep the mother's body moving comfortably
required_materials: A mat or kanga on the floor; a chair for support
activity_description: Once a day, spend five to ten minutes on slow, gentle stretches: roll your shoulders, stretch your arms overhead, gently turn your neck, and stretch your calves while holding a chair. Breathe slowly and never stretch to the point of pain. Avoid lying flat on your back for long late in pregnancy.
cultural_relevance: Can be done at home on a kanga or leso, with no equipment.

developmental_goal: Keep the mother's muscles strong as her body changes in pregnancy
activity_description: Add a few simple strengthening moves to your week: stand up from a chair and sit down slowly ten times, do push-ups against a wall, and rise onto your toes while holding the chair. Move slowly, breathe out as you push, and skip any move that feels uncomfortable.
cultural_relevance: Uses only a chair and a wall, so it fits any home.

activity_name: Getting to Know Baby's Daily Movements
developmental_goal: Recognise the baby's usual movement pattern and act if movements decrease
activity_description: In the third trimester, notice when your baby usually moves, for example after meals or at night. Lie on your side for a few minutes at those times and pay attention to the kicks and rolls. Your baby should move every day: if the movements slow down or stop, contact your clinic straight away.
cultural_relevance: Share the baby's movement pattern with your partner so they can feel the kicks too.

developmental_goal: Ease the mother's body tension and support comfortable rest late in pregnancy
activity_description: When you rest or sleep, use pillows to support your back, bump and knees. Lying on your side with a pillow between your knees is often comfortable later in pregnancy. Change position slowly and get up gradually.
cultural_relevance: Rolled kangas or blankets work well if you don't have many pillows.

developmental_goal: Make regular physical activity easier to keep up through company
activity_description: Arrange to walk with a friend, partner or a group of other expectant mothers a few times a week. Agree on a safe route and a time. Walking together helps you stay active, and it is also a chance to talk and relax.
cultural_relevance: Women's groups, chamas and church groups can organise regular walks.

developmental_goal: Become aware of the baby's developing hearing in the second trimester
activity_description: From the middle of pregnancy, notice how your baby reacts to sounds around you, such as a loud bang, music or voices. Some babies startle or move. Keep a mental note of what the baby seems to notice, and keep very loud noise to a minimum.
cultural_relevance: Everyday sounds at home, in the matatu or at church are enough; there is nothing extra to buy.

developmental_goal: Help the mother relieve discomfort and relax late in pregnancy
required_materials: Music from a phone or radio; a comfortable place to rest
activity_description: When you feel uncomfortable or tired in the last months, take a short break: lie or sit comfortably, put on calming music, and breathe slowly for ten minutes. A short nap or reading can help too.
cultural_relevance: Soft gospel, traditional lullabies or instrumental music all suit a rest break.

developmental_goal: Connect with the baby through touch and notice their responses
activity_description: When you feel the baby kick, press gently on that spot with your hand and wait. Some babies kick back. Talk to the baby as you do it, and let your partner try. Keep the touch gentle and stop if anything feels uncomfortable.
cultural_relevance: A playful way for fathers, siblings and grandparents to feel included.

developmental_goal: Share rhythm and song with the baby before birth
activity_description: Sing a favourite song and gently pat a slow, steady rhythm on your bump in time with the music. Keep the pats very light. Repeat the same song on different days and notice whether the baby moves in response.
cultural_relevance: Clapping and rhythm are part of many Kenyan songs and games, so the baby will hear them often after birth.

activity_name: Asking for Help with Household Work
developmental_goal: Reduce the mother's stress and give her time to rest during pregnancy
activity_description: Sit down with your partner or family and list the household jobs that tire you most, such as carrying water or heavy laundry. Agree who will help with each. Accepting help lets you rest, eat well and look after your feelings, which all affect the baby.
cultural_relevance: Extended family and neighbours often help; asking early makes it easier to share the load.

developmental_goal: Make sure the mother has someone to lean on during pregnancy and after birth
activity_description: Think about who you trust to talk to about your feelings and worries: a partner, sister, friend or community health volunteer. Ask that person to be your support person, and to come with you to some clinic visits if the father can't.
cultural_relevance: Many Kenyan families have a trusted aunt, grandmother or community health volunteer who can take this role.

activity_name: Planning Family Help for After Birth
developmental_goal: Prepare practical support so the mother can rest and care for the newborn
activity_description: Before the birth, plan with the family who will cook, fetch water and look after older children in the first weeks. Write the plan down if it helps. Knowing help is arranged lowers worry and gives you time to rest and bond with the baby.
cultural_relevance: Fits the common practice of relatives helping a new mother during the first weeks.

activity_name: Following a Rattle to One Side
developmental_goal: Help the baby notice and turn towards where sounds come from
required_materials: A rattle or a bottle shaker
activity_description: While the baby lies on their back, gently shake a rattle to one side of their head, out of sight. Wait and see whether they turn their eyes or head towards the sound. Smile and talk when they find it, then try the other side.
cultural_relevance: A small plastic bottle with dry beans and the lid glued shut makes a safe homemade rattle.

developmental_goal: Help the baby follow objects with their eyes
required_materials: A brightly coloured cloth or toy
activity_description: Hold a bright object about 30 centimetres from the baby's face. When they look at it, move it slowly from side to side and watch their eyes follow. Keep it slow and stop when the baby looks away or tires.
cultural_relevance: A brightly patterned kanga or a coloured plastic cup works well.

developmental_goal: Encourage the baby to focus on pictures and faces while hearing talk
required_materials: Brightly coloured pictures, a calendar or family photos
activity_description: Hold a bright picture or a photo of a face where the baby can see it. Talk about what is in the picture in a warm voice, and give the baby time to look. Change the picture every few days to keep it interesting.
cultural_relevance: Calendars, magazines and church bulletins often have bold, colourful pictures.

developmental_goal: Give the baby interesting things to look at and track
required_materials: A clothes hanger, string and light, colourful objects
activity_description: Tie a few light, colourful objects to a clothes hanger with short strings and hang it safely above where the baby lies awake, out of reach. Move it gently now and then so the baby watches it swing. Remove it during sleep and check the strings often.
cultural_relevance: Bottle tops, ribbons and scraps of bright fabric are free materials.

developmental_goal: Help the baby enjoy looking at faces, especially smiling ones
activity_description: Sit with the baby and show them photos of family members or smiling faces in a magazine. Point to each face and say who it is. Babies love faces, so keep the pictures close and give them time to look.
cultural_relevance: A good way to introduce relatives who live far away, such as grandparents upcountry.

activity_name: Tapping the Mirror and Saying Baby's Name
developmental_goal: Help the baby begin to notice their reflection and hear their name
activity_description: Hold a baby-safe mirror where the baby can see it, tap the mirror gently and say their name. Smile and talk about what they see. Keep sessions short and watch for the baby's interest.
cultural_relevance: Any safe, unbreakable mirror or shiny surface can be used.

developmental_goal: Give the baby new things to look at by changing their position
activity_description: When the baby is awake, change their position every so often: on their back, held upright against your shoulder, on their tummy, or on their side with support. Each position gives a new view to look at. Always stay with the baby and put them on their back to sleep.
cultural_relevance: Being carried on a parent's back or front in a kanga offers lots of new views too.

developmental_goal: Help the baby learn the caregiver's voice and face during feeding
activity_description: While feeding, look into the baby's eyes and talk softly to them. Breastfeeding is an especially good time, but bottle feeding can be just as close if you hold the baby and talk. Even newborns can see your face and hear your voice.
cultural_relevance: Talk in the language you speak at home; any warm words help.

activity_name: Talking Through Nappy Changes and Baths
developmental_goal: Fill everyday care with words for the baby to hear
activity_description: During nappy changes, dressing and baths, describe what you are doing: 'Now we take off your vest', 'The water is warm'. Pause and smile so the baby can respond with looks or sounds. These small daily chats add up to many words.
cultural_relevance: Works in any language, and other family members can do it too.

developmental_goal: Help the baby hear lots of words from the first weeks
activity_description: Read aloud to the baby for a few minutes each day, holding them close. The baby won't follow the story yet, but hearing your voice and the rhythm of words builds the foundation for talking later.
cultural_relevance: Use whatever reading material is at home, in Kiswahili, English or the mother tongue.

developmental_goal: Help the baby settle and link a familiar song with sleep
activity_description: Choose one gentle song and sing it softly every time you put the baby down to sleep. Keep the tune slow and calm. Over time the baby connects the song with bedtime, and your familiar voice helps them settle.
cultural_relevance: A traditional lullaby or a song the baby heard before birth works well.

developmental_goal: Start early back-and-forth communication using faces and gestures
activity_description: Hold the baby face to face. When the baby moves their mouth, opens their eyes wide or moves their hands, copy them. Wait to see what they do next and copy again. This back-and-forth is the start of conversation.
cultural_relevance: Needs no materials and can be done during any quiet moment together.

developmental_goal: Show the baby that their signals are noticed and understood
activity_description: Watch for early hunger signals, such as hands to mouth, turning towards the breast or rooting. Respond before the baby cries hard, and say what you notice: 'You're hungry, let's feed.' Babies learn that their signals work.
cultural_relevance: Responsive feeding fits well with keeping the baby close in a kanga or sling.

activity_name: A Tummy Minute After Every Nappy Change
developmental_goal: Build neck and upper-body strength through short, regular tummy time
required_materials: A mat or blanket on the floor
activity_description: After each nappy change, while the baby is awake and calm, place them on their tummy for a minute or two. Get down to their level and talk. Short, frequent sessions add up to more tummy time over the day. Always stay with the baby.
cultural_relevance: A kanga or leso spread on a clean floor makes a good surface.

developmental_goal: Help the baby practise lifting their head while lying on a caregiver
required_materials: A comfortable chair or bed to lean back on
activity_description: Lean back comfortably and lay the baby tummy-down on your chest. Talk and smile so the baby lifts their head to look at you. This is a gentle way to start tummy time, especially for babies who dislike the floor.
cultural_relevance: Fathers and older relatives can do this too, which helps them bond.

developmental_goal: Strengthen the baby's neck and back while being carried
activity_description: Carry the baby tummy-down along your forearm, with their head supported in your hand and your other hand under their body. Walk around slowly so they can look about. Keep one hand on them at all times.
cultural_relevance: A calming hold during fussy evenings, and good practice for lifting the head.

activity_name: Free Kicking Time on a Mat
developmental_goal: Let the baby move their arms and legs freely
activity_description: When the baby is awake, lay them on their back on a mat without tight wrapping so they can kick and wave their arms. Talk and play while they move. Short periods of free movement through the day are good for strength.
cultural_relevance: Out of the kanga carrier for a while, on a clean floor in a safe corner.

developmental_goal: Help the baby feel their arms and legs move during playful care
activity_description: With the baby on their back, gently move their arms up and down and bicycle their legs while you sing or talk. Keep the movements slow and soft, and stop if the baby seems unhappy.
cultural_relevance: Pairs well with action songs or nursery rhymes in any language.

developmental_goal: Help the baby practise grasping and shaking a toy
required_materials: A light rattle or bottle shaker
activity_description: Place a light rattle in the baby's hand and help them close their fingers around it. Shake it gently together, then let them try. Babies first grasp without meaning to, so be patient and keep it playful.
cultural_relevance: A small, sealed plastic bottle with rice or beans is a safe homemade rattle.

developmental_goal: Help the baby feel and enjoy gentle touch on different body parts
activity_description: During nappy changes, gently touch the baby's nose, tummy, hands and feet, saying 'beep' each time. Watch their face as they feel the touch. Babies often come to expect the touch and smile.
cultural_relevance: Name the body parts in the family's language as you go.

developmental_goal: Help the baby listen to and turn towards sounds
required_materials: A small plastic bottle with dry beans, lid glued shut
activity_description: Make a shaker by putting a few dry beans in a small plastic bottle and gluing the lid shut. Shake it slowly side to side above the baby, and let them listen and look. Check the lid each time before use.
cultural_relevance: Made from items found in any Kenyan kitchen at no cost.

developmental_goal: Help the baby feel gentle touch while the caregiver watches their reactions
activity_description: Smile at the baby and gently touch their hands, feet and forehead one at a time. Watch how they wiggle, look or make sounds, and respond to what you see. Stop if they turn away.
cultural_relevance: A calm, simple activity for any family member.

developmental_goal: Help the baby calm down with steady, soft background sound
required_materials: A fan, radio static or gentle shushing
activity_description: When the baby is fussy after their needs are met, try a steady soft sound such as a fan, quiet radio static or your own long 'shhh'. Keep the sound quiet, not loud. Many babies find steady sound calming because it is like the womb.
cultural_relevance: Your own gentle shushing works anywhere, at no cost.

developmental_goal: Help the baby feel snug and calm
required_materials: A thin cotton cloth or kanga
activity_description: Wrap the baby snugly in a thin cloth with their arms in and their hips able to bend and move. Hold and rock them gently. Stop swaddling once the baby can roll, and always lay them on their back to sleep.
cultural_relevance: A light cotton kanga is ideal; avoid heavy blankets in warm weather.

developmental_goal: Soothe the baby with gentle stroking and closeness
required_materials: Clean hands; a little plain oil if you use it
activity_description: With the baby lying on a soft surface or on your lap, stroke their back, arms and legs slowly and gently. Look at them and talk softly. Skin-to-skin time is good too. Stop if the baby seems unsettled.
cultural_relevance: Baby massage is a familiar practice in many Kenyan families.

developmental_goal: Help the baby feel safe and loved through holding and cuddling
activity_description: Hold and cuddle the baby often, and pick them up when they cry. Holding and responding to a young baby won't spoil them; it teaches them they are safe. Carrying the baby close during the day is a good way to do this.
cultural_relevance: Carrying the baby on your back or front in a kanga keeps them close while you work.

developmental_goal: Help caregivers understand the baby's feelings and needs from their cues
activity_description: Watch the baby closely during the day and notice the signals they give: looking at you when they want to play, turning away when they need a break, or rubbing their eyes when tired. Respond to what you see, and share what you learn with other carers.
cultural_relevance: Grandmothers and older siblings can learn the baby's signals too.

developmental_goal: Respond to the baby's fullness signals during feeds
activity_description: During feeds, watch for signs that the baby has had enough, such as turning away, slowing down or closing their mouth. It is fine to stop when the baby isn't hungry. Responding to these signals helps them trust you.
cultural_relevance: Fits both breastfeeding and cup or bottle feeding.

activity_name: Staying Calm When Crying Is Hard
developmental_goal: Keep the caregiver and baby calm and safe during long crying
required_materials: A safe place to lay the baby, such as a cot
activity_description: When the baby cries for a long time, try speaking softly, holding, rocking or singing. If you start to feel angry or overwhelmed, lay the baby on their back somewhere safe, step away for a few minutes, and check on them every five to ten minutes. Never shake a baby.
cultural_relevance: Ask a family member or neighbour to take a turn so you can rest.

developmental_goal: Give the baby the caregiver's full attention during time together
activity_description: Set aside some time each day when your phone is put away and you simply hold, look at and talk to the baby. Babies notice when you respond to them, and these focused moments help them feel connected to you.
cultural_relevance: Mealtimes and evening rest are good moments to put phones aside.

developmental_goal: Help the baby begin to learn ways to calm themselves
activity_description: Notice what helps the baby calm down, such as sucking on their fingers or hands. Let them use these ways to settle, while staying close and comforting them when they need you. Over time they learn to calm themselves a little.
cultural_relevance: Works alongside carrying and comforting, which remain important.

developmental_goal: Help the baby discover that things can be pulled out of a container
required_materials: An empty wipes box or tin; squares of colourful fabric
activity_description: Push a few squares of colourful fabric into an empty wipes box or a tin with a smooth opening, leaving a corner showing. Show the baby how to pull one out, then let them try. Cheer each time a new colour appears, and refill the box together.
cultural_relevance: Off-cuts of kitenge or kanga fabric make bright, free squares.

developmental_goal: Help the baby learn that their actions make things happen
activity_description: When the baby drops a toy, pick it up, say 'Here it is!' and hand it back. Babies drop things on purpose to see what happens, so treat it as a game. Name what happened each time: 'Down it went! Back it comes!'
cultural_relevance: Older siblings often enjoy playing this game with the baby.

activity_name: Reaching for a Ring on a String
developmental_goal: Encourage the baby to look at, reach for and explore a dangling object
required_materials: A large ring or bangle tied to a short string
activity_description: Tie a big, safe ring to a short piece of string. Hold it above the baby so they can see it, and move it slowly. Let them reach for it, touch it and pull it. Always hold the string yourself and put it away after play.
cultural_relevance: A plastic bangle or a large wooden curtain ring works well.

developmental_goal: Help the baby watch how objects move when they roll, drop and bounce
required_materials: Soft, colourful balls of different textures
activity_description: Sit with the baby supported and show them how a soft ball rolls across the floor, drops from your hand and bounces. Let them touch and hold the balls. Say what each ball is doing as it moves.
cultural_relevance: A homemade ball of tightly tied cloth or plastic bags is a common local alternative.

developmental_goal: Help the baby explore an easy-to-hold book with bright pictures
required_materials: A cloth book or a sturdy picture card
activity_description: Give the baby an easy-to-hold cloth book or picture card with bright pictures. Let them hold it, look at it and mouth it. Point to the pictures and name them, and follow the baby's interest.
cultural_relevance: A homemade book of bright pictures glued on card works if cloth books are not available.

developmental_goal: Help the baby link words to new things seen outside the home
activity_description: When you go out with the baby, point out and name the new things you see: 'Look, a car!', 'That's a cow', 'See the tree?' Speak slowly and give them time to look. Everyday trips are full of words to share.
cultural_relevance: Trips to the market, shamba, church or clinic all offer plenty to name.

developmental_goal: Encourage the baby to babble back and forth while looking at pictures
required_materials: Colourful pictures, a book or a magazine
activity_description: Every day, look at colourful pictures with the baby. Talk about what you see, and when the baby babbles, answer as if they are talking to you. Keep the back-and-forth going for as long as they enjoy it.
cultural_relevance: Any colourful pictures at home will do, in any language.

activity_name: Talking About What Baby Is Looking At
developmental_goal: Connect words with whatever holds the baby's attention
activity_description: Watch where the baby is looking and point to the same thing. Name it and say something about it: 'That's the cat. The cat is sleeping.' Following the baby's interest makes the words easier to learn.
cultural_relevance: Works at home, in the compound or while being carried in a kanga.

activity_name: A Quiet Time for Books and Songs
developmental_goal: Build a calm daily time for reading and singing
required_materials: A book or a few favourite songs
activity_description: Choose a quiet time each day, such as before a nap, to read or sing with the baby. Hold them close, keep your voice gentle and repeat favourite songs. A regular quiet time helps the baby settle and hear lots of language.
cultural_relevance: Mother-tongue lullabies and songs can be part of the routine.

developmental_goal: Build early communication through shared smiles, laughs and talk
activity_description: Spend a few minutes face to face, smiling, laughing and talking with the baby. When they coo or smile, respond warmly and add more words. Copy their sounds now and then to get a conversation going.
cultural_relevance: No materials needed; any carer can do it.

developmental_goal: Support the baby's language and brain development with daily singing and music
required_materials: None, or music from a radio or phone
activity_description: Sing to the baby several times a day, during baths, feeds or play, and play music they can listen to. Repeat the same songs often so they become familiar. Watch for the baby's smiles and sounds as they join in.
cultural_relevance: Traditional and church songs in the family's language are a rich source.

developmental_goal: Help the baby push with their legs and feel their weight on their feet
activity_description: Sit down and hold the baby under the arms with their feet on your lap. Let them push and bounce gently as you sing or count. Support them fully and keep it short and fun.
cultural_relevance: A favourite game with grandparents and older siblings, paired with a bouncing song.

activity_name: Rolling Over to Reach a Toy
developmental_goal: Encourage the baby to roll over by placing toys just out of reach
activity_description: During tummy time or back time, place a favourite toy just out of reach to one side. Encourage the baby to reach and roll towards it, and cheer every effort. Let them get the toy in the end so it stays fun.
cultural_relevance: A bright cloth or shaker made from a bottle works as a target toy.

developmental_goal: Help the baby practise sitting upright and balancing
activity_description: Hold the baby upright in a sitting position, or sit them in your lap facing out, and give them toys to hold and look at. As they get steadier, support them a little less while staying ready to catch. Keep sessions short.
cultural_relevance: Rolled kangas or cushions can give extra support around the baby.

developmental_goal: Help the baby feel their legs take weight while they look around
activity_description: Hold the baby under the arms so their feet rest on the floor or your lap and they take some weight on their legs. Turn slowly and name the things you can both see. Keep it short and fully supported.
cultural_relevance: A chance to look out of the window or around the compound together.

developmental_goal: Help the baby practise reaching for, batting and grasping objects
required_materials: A light scarf or soft cloth
activity_description: While the baby lies on their back, hold a light scarf just above their chest and move it slowly. Let them swipe, bat and grab at it. Move it to different sides so they reach with both hands.
cultural_relevance: A light kanga or chiffon scarf is easy to swipe at and grab.

developmental_goal: Give the baby plenty of time to move and explore freely
activity_description: Each day, give the baby time on a mat on the floor rather than long periods in a seat, bouncer or carrier. Lie down with them and play. Floor time lets them stretch, roll, reach and kick.
cultural_relevance: A kanga on a clean floor in a safe corner of the house works well.

developmental_goal: Help the baby feel and explore different textures
activity_description: Gather pieces of fabric that feel different, such as soft cotton, knitted wool, rough denim and smooth satin. Let the baby touch each one with their hands and feet while you describe it: soft, rough, smooth.
cultural_relevance: Pieces of kitenge, knitted sweaters and old jeans give a range of textures.

developmental_goal: Let the baby explore safe objects with their mouth
required_materials: Clean, safe objects too big to swallow
activity_description: Offer the baby clean, safe things to mouth, such as a teething ring, a large wooden spoon or a cloth. Babies learn about objects by mouthing them. Check that nothing is sharp, hot or small enough to choke on.
cultural_relevance: Wash household objects well before giving them to the baby.

developmental_goal: Help the baby hear and enjoy many different sounds and voices
activity_description: Play with different sounds: whisper, clap, click your tongue, hum and make funny noises. Watch how the baby reacts and repeat the ones they like. Let other family members add their voices too.
cultural_relevance: Fun for older siblings to join in with their own funny noises.

developmental_goal: Help the baby enjoy gentle movement and build balance
activity_description: Holding the baby securely, lift them slowly up and down, sway gently side to side and turn them to face different ways. Watch their face and slow down if they seem unsure. Keep movements smooth and gentle.
cultural_relevance: Pairs well with a lifting song or a counting rhyme.

developmental_goal: Help the baby enjoy the feel and sound of water
required_materials: A baby basin with warm water
activity_description: During bath time, let the baby kick and pat the water while you hold them securely. Pour a little water gently over their tummy and say what it feels like. Never leave the baby alone in water, even for a moment.
cultural_relevance: A plastic basin used for baby baths in most Kenyan homes is all you need.

developmental_goal: Share music and gentle movement with the baby
required_materials: Music from a radio or phone, or your own singing
activity_description: Hold the baby close and sway, bounce gently or dance slowly to music. Change the pace with different songs and watch how the baby responds. Keep the volume comfortable.
cultural_relevance: Any music the family enjoys, from benga to gospel, works.

developmental_goal: Learn the baby's likes and dislikes by watching their reactions
activity_description: Pay attention to how the baby reacts to different things: songs, toys, people, being outside. Notice what makes them smile and what makes them fuss. Offer more of what they enjoy, and share what you learn with other carers.
cultural_relevance: A good way for fathers and grandparents to get to know the baby.

developmental_goal: Help the baby feel understood when they are upset
activity_description: Watch for changes in the baby's mood. When they are upset, stop what you are doing, pick them up and comfort them. Say what you think they feel: 'You're upset. I'm here.' Taking a break together helps them settle.
cultural_relevance: Comforting promptly is a natural part of carrying and caring for babies.

developmental_goal: Help the baby learn to calm down with the caregiver's support
activity_description: When the baby is upset, try soft talking, holding, rocking, singing or offering a favourite toy. Notice which ways work best for this baby and use them consistently. Your calm helps the baby calm.
cultural_relevance: A familiar cloth or kanga with the mother's smell can be comforting.

developmental_goal: Build the baby's social skills through playful back-and-forth smiles
activity_description: Sit face to face with the baby and smile. When they smile back, smile bigger and say something cheerful. Copy their expressions and sounds and wait for them to respond. Keep the game going as long as they enjoy it.
cultural_relevance: Any family member can play, which helps the baby build relationships.

activity_name: Smiles and Talk During Daily Care
developmental_goal: Help the baby feel loved and connected during everyday care
activity_description: During feeds, baths and nappy changes, hold the baby close, look at them, smile and talk. Everyday care is full of chances to show love. Slow down a little and enjoy these moments together.
cultural_relevance: Fits naturally into daily routines in any home.

developmental_goal: Enjoy making music together as a family with the baby
activity_description: Gather the family for a few minutes of music: sing, clap, pat your knees or tap a pot with a wooden spoon while the baby watches and listens from a lap. Let the baby hold a shaker. Making music together builds closeness.
cultural_relevance: Family singing and clapping are part of many Kenyan homes and celebrations.

developmental_goal: Help the baby learn that their actions make sounds
required_materials: A metal pot and a wooden spoon
activity_description: Give the baby a metal pot and a wooden spoon and show them how to bang it. Let them bang, drop and handle it. Copy their rhythm on another pot, then let them copy yours.
cultural_relevance: A sufuria and a mwiko are found in every Kenyan kitchen.

developmental_goal: Help the baby explore opening, closing and dropping things into containers
required_materials: Clean plastic containers with lids; safe objects too big to swallow
activity_description: Give the baby a few clean containers with lids and some safe objects to put inside. Show them how to drop things in, shake them and take the lid off. Let them explore freely, and name what they do.
cultural_relevance: Empty margarine tubs or plastic jars with lids make good containers.

developmental_goal: Help the baby learn to search for hidden objects
required_materials: Two plastic cups; a small toy
activity_description: While the baby watches, hide a toy under one of two upside-down cups. Ask 'Where did it go?' and let them lift the cup to find it. Start with one cup, then use two as they get the idea.
cultural_relevance: Plastic cups or small sufurias from the kitchen work well.

developmental_goal: Help the baby enjoy cause and effect as objects fall and come back
activity_description: When the baby drops a toy from their seat or lap, make a game of it: say 'Uh oh, it fell!' and hand it back. Babies learn about falling and finding by repeating this many times.
cultural_relevance: Older siblings usually love being part of this game.

developmental_goal: Help the baby explore stacking, knocking down and filling
activity_description: Stack two or three blocks or containers and let the baby knock them down or dump them out of a box. Stack them again together. Babies love repeating this, and they learn how objects fit and fall.
cultural_relevance: Empty boxes and plastic cups from the kitchen make good stacking toys.

developmental_goal: Help the baby notice objects both close by and far away
required_materials: A toy; a window or open view
activity_description: Show the baby a toy close to them, then point to something further away, such as a bird or a tree, and name it. Move between near and far things, giving the baby time to look at each.
cultural_relevance: The view from a doorway or veranda is ideal for this game.

activity_name: Turning the Pages of a Board Book
developmental_goal: Help the baby explore a sturdy book by turning its pages
required_materials: A chunky board book or card pages
activity_description: Sit with the baby and a sturdy board book. Let them try to turn the pages, even several at once, and name the pictures they see. Follow their pace and let them explore the book in their own way.
cultural_relevance: Sturdy card pages tied together make a homemade alternative.

developmental_goal: Help the baby move from babbling to words
activity_description: When the baby makes a sound like 'ba', repeat it and add a simple word: 'Ba! Ball!' Repeat the sounds they make and keep adding words that match. Smile and wait for them to try again.
cultural_relevance: Use words in the language the family speaks most at home.

developmental_goal: Help the baby communicate with gestures
activity_description: Show the baby simple gestures and use them every day: wave bye-bye when someone leaves, shake your head for 'no', clap when something is good. Say the word as you do the gesture and help them copy.
cultural_relevance: Waving 'kwaheri' to visitors gives plenty of practice.

developmental_goal: Help the baby learn the names of the people around them
activity_description: Point to family members and name them: 'That's Dada', 'Here's Shosho'. Use photos for relatives who live far away. Ask 'Where's Baba?' and see if the baby looks.
cultural_relevance: Use the family's own names for relatives, such as Shosho, Guka, Mama or Baba.

developmental_goal: Give the baby simple hand signs to show what they want
activity_description: Choose two or three simple signs, such as 'more', 'milk' and 'all done', and use them with the word every time. For 'more', tap your fingertips together. Help the baby make the sign and respond when they use it.
cultural_relevance: Make up simple signs that fit the family's words and routines.

developmental_goal: Help the baby learn to respond when called by name
activity_description: Call the baby's name from a little distance in a cheerful voice. When they turn to look, smile and say 'There you are!' Use their name often in everyday talk.
cultural_relevance: Use the name the family uses most at home, including pet names.

activity_name: Passing a Spoon from Hand to Hand
developmental_goal: Help the baby practise passing objects from one hand to the other
required_materials: A wooden spoon or small toy
activity_description: Give the baby a wooden spoon in one hand and show them how to pass it to the other. Offer it to alternate hands. Praise each try and let them explore the spoon in their own way.
cultural_relevance: A small mwiko or plastic spoon is ideal.

developmental_goal: Help the baby safely practise pulling up to stand
activity_description: Make sure the baby has sturdy, stable furniture they can safely pull up on, such as a low table or sofa. Place a toy on top to encourage them. Stay close and remove anything that could tip over or fall.
cultural_relevance: A heavy wooden stool or low table that won't tip works well.

developmental_goal: Help the baby practise picking up food with their fingers
activity_description: Offer soft, small pieces of safe food for the baby to pick up and feed themselves. Expect mess, and stay with them throughout. Avoid foods that are choking hazards, such as whole groundnuts or hard raw pieces.
cultural_relevance: Soft ripe banana, well-cooked sweet potato or avocado are easy local finger foods.

developmental_goal: Help the baby use both hands together to explore a toy
required_materials: A toy big enough to need two hands
activity_description: Give the baby a toy that is easiest to hold with two hands, such as a ball or a container. Let them turn it, shake it and pass it around. Sit with them and describe what they are doing.
cultural_relevance: A plastic bowl or a soft homemade ball is a good size.

developmental_goal: Help the baby learn how much effort different objects need
activity_description: Offer the baby a few safe objects that weigh different amounts, such as a light cup, a small cloth bag of beans and a wooden block. Let them pick up and move each one. Say 'heavy' or 'light' as they handle them.
cultural_relevance: A small, tightly sewn cloth bag of beans makes a safe heavy object.

activity_name: New Tastes and Textures at Mealtimes
developmental_goal: Help the baby get used to a variety of tastes and textures
required_materials: A variety of soft family foods
activity_description: Offer the baby small amounts of different family foods with different tastes and textures, such as smooth, mashed and soft lumpy. If they refuse a food, try it again on another day. Let them touch and explore their food.
cultural_relevance: Mashed pumpkin, sweet potato, avocado, ripe banana and soft githeri suit this age.

developmental_goal: Help the baby notice their body in a mirror as parts are named
activity_description: Sit with the baby in front of a mirror. Touch and name their nose, eyes, hands and feet, and point to the same parts in the mirror. Make funny faces together and watch them react.
cultural_relevance: Name body parts in the family's language, such as pua, macho and mkono.

developmental_goal: Help the baby feel new textures with their hands
required_materials: A clean sponge, a cloth and other safe textured items
activity_description: Give the baby a clean sponge, a soft cloth and other safe items with different textures to squeeze and explore. Describe each one: squishy, soft, bumpy. Supervise closely and keep small items away.
cultural_relevance: A new kitchen sponge or a loofah offers an interesting texture.

developmental_goal: Help the baby notice which objects make noise and which are quiet
required_materials: Safe items that crinkle, rattle or are silent
activity_description: Put out a few safe objects: some that crinkle or rattle, like a sealed bottle of beans or a paper bag, and some that are quiet, like a cloth. Let the baby explore them and notice which ones make sounds.
cultural_relevance: Everyday kitchen items make good noisy and quiet objects.

developmental_goal: Share rhythm and music with the baby using the body
activity_description: Make music without instruments: clap, stomp, snap your fingers and pat your thighs to a rhythm. Help the baby clap their hands or pat the floor with you. Change the speed from slow to fast.
cultural_relevance: Clapping games and songs are familiar in many Kenyan families.

activity_name: Treasure Basket of Shapes and Textures
developmental_goal: Help the baby explore objects of different shapes, sizes and textures
required_materials: A basket with safe household objects
activity_description: Fill a low basket with safe household objects of different shapes, sizes and textures, such as a wooden spoon, a small cloth, a plastic cup and a large lid. Sit nearby while the baby explores. Swap objects often.
cultural_relevance: A kiondo basket filled with kitchen items is a classic local treasure basket.

developmental_goal: Help the baby feel secure when caregivers leave and return
activity_description: When you need to leave the baby with someone, say a short, cheerful goodbye rather than slipping away. When you come back, greet them warmly and tell them you're back. This builds trust that you return.
cultural_relevance: Helpful when the baby is left with grandparents or a house help.

activity_name: Passing a Toy Back and Forth
developmental_goal: Help the baby enjoy taking turns with a caregiver
activity_description: Sit facing the baby and hand them a toy, then hold out your hand and ask for it back. Pass it back and forth, saying 'My turn, your turn.' Praise them when they give it to you.
cultural_relevance: A simple game that brothers and sisters can play too.

activity_name: Saying What You Want Them to Do
developmental_goal: Help the baby understand which behaviour the caregiver wants
activity_description: Instead of saying 'Don't stand up', say what you want: 'Time to sit.' Use short, positive words and show them what to do. Praise them when they do it.
cultural_relevance: Works with all carers; agree on the same words as a family.

developmental_goal: Help the child learn what everyday objects are for by imitating the caregiver
required_materials: Everyday objects such as a hat, a comb and a cup
activity_description: Show the child an everyday object, such as a hat, and show how it is used by putting it on your head. Hand it to them and see if they copy you. Try other objects like a comb or a cup, and cheer their attempts.
cultural_relevance: Use familiar items from home, such as a kofia, a comb or a small sufuria.

developmental_goal: Help the child learn how things fit inside each other
required_materials: Cups or containers of different sizes
activity_description: Give the child three or four cups or containers of different sizes. Show them how the small ones fit inside the big ones, then take them out again. Let them try, and talk about big and small as they play.
cultural_relevance: Plastic cups and small sufurias of different sizes work well.

developmental_goal: Help the child practise putting objects in and taking them out of a container
required_materials: A clean tin or plastic container; wooden clothes pegs
activity_description: Give the child a clean container and a handful of clothes pegs. Show them how to drop the pegs in and tip them out again. As they get better, cut a slot in a plastic lid for posting the pegs through.
cultural_relevance: Wooden clothes pegs and an empty Kimbo or margarine tin are common at home.

developmental_goal: Help the child explore books with flaps and textures
required_materials: A book with flaps or textures, or a homemade one
activity_description: Read a book with flaps to lift or textures to touch, and let the child find what is under each flap. Talk about the pictures. If you don't have one, glue paper flaps over pictures in a homemade book.
cultural_relevance: Homemade books with flaps cut from paper or card cost almost nothing.

developmental_goal: Help the child enjoy searching for and finding a hidden person
activity_description: Hide behind a door or curtain where the child can easily find you, and call their name. When they find you, celebrate together. Take turns so they hide and you look for them.
cultural_relevance: A favourite game with older siblings in the house or compound.

developmental_goal: Help the child follow the caregiver's attention to interesting things
activity_description: Point to interesting things around you, such as a bird, a car or a cow, and say 'Look!' Wait for the child to follow your finger and look. Name what you see together and talk about it.
cultural_relevance: Walks to the market or around the village offer many things to point at.

developmental_goal: Help the child learn new words by building on the ones they already say
activity_description: When the child says a word or part of a word, repeat it clearly and add a little more. If they say 'ba', say 'Ball! A red ball!' Keep your words simple, and smile to show you understood them.
cultural_relevance: Works in any language spoken at home.

developmental_goal: Encourage the child to try saying the names of things they point to
activity_description: When the child points to something, name it, then wait a few seconds to see if they make a sound. Whatever sound they make, respond warmly and say the name again.
cultural_relevance: A good habit for every carer, from parents to grandparents.

developmental_goal: Help the child learn the names of family, friends and pets
activity_description: Make a simple book with photos of family members, friends and pets, including one of the child. Look at it together and name each person. Ask 'Where's Shosho?' and let them point.
cultural_relevance: Printed phone photos or pictures from family events make a precious homemade book.

developmental_goal: Help the child learn words for everyday activities
activity_description: Talk through daily routines as you do them and make up short songs about them: a washing-hands song, a getting-dressed song. Use the same songs every day so the child learns the words.
cultural_relevance: Make up songs in Kiswahili or the mother tongue to familiar tunes.

developmental_goal: Invite the child to talk and pretend using a soft toy
activity_description: Hold a soft toy and pretend it is talking to the child: 'Hello! What are you eating?' Give the child their own toy and see if they talk back or copy you. Keep the voices playful.
cultural_relevance: A homemade cloth doll works as well as a bought one.

activity_name: A New Book After a Favourite
developmental_goal: Introduce the child to new words and ideas through books
activity_description: Read the child's favourite book, then read a new one straight after. The familiar book settles them, and the new one brings new words and ideas. Talk about the pictures in both.
cultural_relevance: Library books, church picture books and community reading corners can provide new books.

developmental_goal: Help the child practise walking by pushing something sturdy
required_materials: A sturdy box or push toy
activity_description: Give the child a sturdy push toy or an empty cardboard box to push across the floor. Clear a safe path and stay nearby. Pushing helps new walkers steady themselves and take more steps.
cultural_relevance: A strong carton box filled with a little weight is a free push toy.

developmental_goal: Help the child learn to drink from a cup without a lid
required_materials: A small open cup with a little water
activity_description: Give the child a small open cup with a little water at mealtimes. Help them hold it with both hands and tip it slowly. Expect spills, and praise them for trying.
cultural_relevance: A small plastic or tin cup is ideal.

developmental_goal: Help the child learn to feed themselves with a spoon
required_materials: A child-sized spoon; thick, soft food
activity_description: Give the child their own spoon and a bowl of thick, soft food that sticks to the spoon. Let them try to scoop and feed themselves, helping when needed. It will be messy, and that's fine.
cultural_relevance: Thick porridge, mashed potatoes or soft githeri are easy to scoop.

developmental_goal: Help the child step sideways while holding on to steady furniture
required_materials: Sturdy furniture at about the child's chest height
activity_description: Arrange sturdy furniture, such as a sofa and a low table, so the child can hold on and step sideways along it. Place a toy at one end to encourage them. Stay close and remove anything that could tip.
cultural_relevance: A heavy wooden bench or sofa works well; check it won't slide.

developmental_goal: Help the child practise squatting and standing up again
activity_description: Scatter a few toys on the floor while the child is standing. Encourage them to squat down, pick one up and stand again, and to put it in a basket. Stay nearby in case they wobble.
cultural_relevance: Turn tidying up into this game after play.

developmental_goal: Help the child watch, chase and touch bubbles
required_materials: Bubble mixture (soap and water) and a wand
activity_description: Blow bubbles for the child to watch, reach for and pop. Name what happens: 'Up, up! Pop!' Keep the mixture out of their mouth and eyes.
cultural_relevance: Make bubble mixture from dish soap and water, with a wand from bent wire.

developmental_goal: Help the child explore a soft, squishy texture with their hands
required_materials: Shaving cream or thick soap foam; a plastic-covered table
activity_description: Cover a table with plastic and spread a little shaving cream or thick soap foam on it. Let the child squish it, draw in it and explore with their hands, brushes or spoons. Keep it away from their eyes and mouth, and wash hands afterwards.
cultural_relevance: Thick foam from bar soap is a cheap alternative to shaving cream.

developmental_goal: Help the child explore objects of different sizes, textures and colours
required_materials: A bucket; blocks or objects too big to swallow
activity_description: Fill a bucket with blocks or objects of different sizes, textures and colours, all too big to swallow. Let the child take them out, feel them and put them back. Describe each one as they explore.
cultural_relevance: Wooden off-cuts sanded smooth, corn cobs and large lids make good blocks.

developmental_goal: Help the child fill and pour water during bath time
activity_description: Bring a cup into the bath and show the child how to fill it and pour it out. Let them pour over their hands, tummy and the water. Stay with them the whole time they are in water.
cultural_relevance: A plastic cup in the family basin is all you need.

developmental_goal: Help the child explore loud and soft sounds with homemade instruments
required_materials: Pots, lids, spoons, sealed bottles of beans
activity_description: Set out pots, lids, wooden spoons and sealed bottle shakers. Let the child bang, shake and tap them, and show them how to play loudly and softly. Join in with a song.
cultural_relevance: Sufurias, sufuria lids and bottle shakers make a full home band.

developmental_goal: Help the child enjoy music and moving to the beat
activity_description: Sing or play children's and family songs and dance together. Hold hands, sway, stamp and clap. Let the child lead some moves and copy them.
cultural_relevance: Children's songs and family favourites in any language work well.

developmental_goal: Help the child feel capable by helping with small tasks
required_materials: Everyday items like shoes, socks and a basket
activity_description: Ask the child to help with small tasks: fetch their shoes, put socks in a basket or carry a light snack bag. Show them what to do and thank them warmly when they help.
cultural_relevance: Helping with family tasks is valued in many Kenyan homes from an early age.

developmental_goal: Help the child learn gentle behaviour through praise
activity_description: Show the child how to touch gently, for example stroking a pet or a baby softly. When they are gentle, praise them and give a hug. Praise works better than scolding for teaching kind behaviour.
cultural_relevance: Useful around younger siblings, chickens, cats or dogs at home.

developmental_goal: Guide the child to safe play without harsh words
activity_description: When the child goes for something unsafe, calmly offer a different toy or move them to another activity. Save a firm 'no' for real danger. Avoid shouting or smacking; redirecting is calmer and works better.
cultural_relevance: A helpful approach for all carers, including grandparents and house helps.

activity_name: A Comfort Item for a New Carer
developmental_goal: Help the child feel safe when left with a new carer
activity_description: When the child is going to spend time with a new carer, send along a favourite toy or cloth that comforts them. Show the carer how the child likes to be comforted. Familiar things help them settle.
cultural_relevance: Helpful when starting with a new house help or day care.

developmental_goal: Help the child enjoy putting toys away together
required_materials: A basket or box for toys
activity_description: Make up a short tidy-up song and sing it every time you put toys away together. Show the child where things go and help them. Praise every toy they put away.
cultural_relevance: Make up the song to a familiar Kiswahili or English tune.

developmental_goal: Help the child begin pretend play with a soft toy
required_materials: A soft toy or doll; a spoon and bowl
activity_description: Show the child how to pretend to feed a soft toy with a spoon. Take turns feeding it, and talk about what teddy is eating. Let the child add their own ideas, such as putting teddy to bed.
cultural_relevance: A homemade cloth doll and kitchen items make perfect pretend toys.

developmental_goal: Help the child practise making simple choices
activity_description: Offer the child a choice between two things, such as two shirts or two snacks: 'Red shirt or blue shirt?' Hold them up so they can point. Accept their choice and name it.
cultural_relevance: Works with everyday choices like two fruits or two cups.

developmental_goal: Help the child find out which things float and which sink
required_materials: A basin of water; safe objects such as a leaf, a stone, a cork and a spoon
activity_description: Fill a basin with water. Have the child collect a few safe objects and drop them in one at a time to see which float and which sink. Say the result each time. Stay with the child near water at all times.
cultural_relevance: Leaves, bottle tops, stones and spoons from the compound make good test objects.

activity_name: Roll It, Push It, Put It In
developmental_goal: Help the child explore how objects move and fit
required_materials: A ball, blocks and a box
activity_description: Play rolling, pushing and container games: roll a ball across the floor, push a block along, and put blocks in and out of a box. Name the actions as you play: roll, push, in, out.
cultural_relevance: Use any household box and homemade balls or blocks.

activity_name: Simple Questions About What They See
developmental_goal: Help the child think about and answer simple questions
activity_description: Ask simple questions about what the child can see: 'What's that?', 'Where is the dog?', 'What is Mama doing?' Give them time to answer by pointing or with words, and fill in the word if they need help.
cultural_relevance: Ask in Kiswahili or the mother tongue during walks or meals.

developmental_goal: Help the child see the caregiver's face and understand speech
activity_description: When you talk to the child, get down to their eye level by kneeling or sitting. Look at them and speak clearly. Seeing your face helps them understand you and copy how you say words.
cultural_relevance: A small change every family member can make.

developmental_goal: Help the child learn the names of body parts
activity_description: Point to body parts on the child and on yourself and name them: nose, ears, tummy, toes. Ask 'Where's your nose?' and celebrate when they point. Bath and dressing times are good moments for this.
cultural_relevance: Name body parts in two languages if the family uses both.

developmental_goal: Help the child put words together into short sentences
activity_description: When the child says one word, add a word or two to make a short sentence. If they say 'milk', say 'More milk' or 'Milk, please'. Keep it natural and don't make them repeat it.
cultural_relevance: Works in any language spoken at home.

developmental_goal: Help the child learn words for actions and descriptions in picture books
activity_description: Read a picture book together and describe what is happening in simple words: 'The boy is running', 'The big cow eats grass'. Point as you talk and let the child turn the pages.
cultural_relevance: Picture books in Kiswahili and local languages are increasingly available.

developmental_goal: Help the child learn animal names and sounds while moving
activity_description: Move around the room like different animals, a waddling duck or a slithering snake, and ask the child what sound each animal makes. Make the sounds together and name each animal.
cultural_relevance: Include familiar animals such as a cow, goat, chicken and dog.

developmental_goal: Help the child walk while pushing or pulling a toy
required_materials: A push toy, or a box on a string
activity_description: Give the child a toy to push or pull as they walk, such as a box tied to a short string. Clear a safe path and let them walk around the room or compound. Keep strings short and supervise.
cultural_relevance: A tin or small box on a string makes a simple pull toy.

developmental_goal: Build the child's strength and balance with animal walks
activity_description: Show the child how to bear walk on hands and feet with their bottom up, and how to duck walk by squatting low and waddling. Take turns being different animals and keep it playful.
cultural_relevance: Fun to play outside with siblings and neighbours.

activity_name: Tossing a Ball into a Bucket
developmental_goal: Help the child practise aiming and throwing
required_materials: A soft ball or bean bag; a bucket or basket
activity_description: Place a bucket a short distance from the child and show them how to toss a soft ball or bean bag into it. Move the bucket closer or further as needed. Cheer every throw.
cultural_relevance: A homemade ball of tied plastic bags and a plastic basin work well.

developmental_goal: Help the child climb, crawl and step through a simple course
required_materials: Cushions, a blanket and a table
activity_description: Set up a short course: climb over a pile of cushions, crawl under a table covered with a blanket and step over a rolled-up mat. Go through it together first, then let the child try. Stay close.
cultural_relevance: Uses household items such as cushions, mats and a table.

developmental_goal: Help the child practise balance by walking along a line
required_materials: A line drawn in the soil or made with tape or a rope
activity_description: Make a line on the ground with a stick in the soil, a rope or tape, and show the child how to walk along it. Walk beside them and offer support at the trunk if they wobble. Make it longer as they improve.
cultural_relevance: A line drawn in the compound soil costs nothing.

developmental_goal: Build the child's walking strength and coordination
activity_description: Take regular short walks together, letting the child walk part of the way. Stop to look at things along the route. Walking on different surfaces, like grass and paths, builds strength and balance.
cultural_relevance: Walks to a neighbour, church or the shop are good opportunities.

developmental_goal: Help the child enjoy the splash and sound of objects dropped in water
required_materials: A basin of water; smooth stones too big to swallow
activity_description: Give the child a few smooth stones, too big to swallow, and a basin of water. Let them drop the stones in and watch the splash and ripples. Talk about the sound and the splash. Stay with them near water.
cultural_relevance: Smooth river stones from the compound work well.

developmental_goal: Help the child feel how sand and water change when mixed
required_materials: A basin, sand and a cup of water
activity_description: Put some sand in a basin and let the child feel it dry. Then add a little water and let them mix it with their hands or a spoon. Talk about how it feels: dry and soft, then wet and sticky.
cultural_relevance: Clean sand or soil from the compound makes great sensory play.

developmental_goal: Help the child feel and watch water as they scoop and pour
required_materials: A basin of water; plastic cups, spoons and a funnel
activity_description: At bath time or with a basin of water, give the child plastic cups, spoons and a funnel. Let them scoop and pour, and watch the water run through the funnel and over their hands. Stay with them near water at all times.
cultural_relevance: The top of a plastic bottle, cut off and turned upside down, makes a good funnel.

developmental_goal: Help the child notice living things in and around water
activity_description: On a walk near a pond, stream or water tank, stop to look for frogs, fish, insects or birds. Point them out and name them. Keep the child's hand firmly in yours near water.
cultural_relevance: Rainy-season puddles and ponds often have frogs and insects to watch.

developmental_goal: Help the child explore and talk about things found in nature
activity_description: Go outside together and collect a few safe natural things: leaves, smooth stones, feathers, flowers. Back home, look at and feel each one together and talk about it: rough, smooth, soft, green.
cultural_relevance: Leaves, seeds and stones from around the home or shamba are free and familiar.

developmental_goal: Help the child enjoy moving to music
required_materials: Music from a radio or phone
activity_description: Put on lively music and have a dance party. Clap, spin, jump and stomp together, and freeze when the music stops. Let the child choose some songs.
cultural_relevance: Popular children's songs and Kenyan music make it fun for the whole family.

activity_name: Praising What You Want to See
developmental_goal: Help the child learn which behaviour the caregiver likes through praise
activity_description: Notice and praise the child when they do something you want to see more of, such as sharing, sitting at the table or being gentle. Be specific: 'You gave your sister the ball. That was kind.' Praise more than you correct.
cultural_relevance: All carers can use the same words of praise for consistency.

developmental_goal: Help the child notice others' feelings and respond kindly
activity_description: When someone is sad, happy or hurt, point it out to the child: 'Your brother is sad. He fell.' Suggest a kind response, such as a hug or a gentle pat, and do it together.
cultural_relevance: Caring for siblings and neighbours' children gives many chances to practise.

developmental_goal: Help the child practise waiting and taking turns
activity_description: Blow bubbles for the child to pop, then let them try blowing while you pop. Say 'My turn, your turn' as you swap. Turn-taking games teach waiting in a fun way.
cultural_relevance: Homemade soap bubbles cost very little.

developmental_goal: Help the child calm down in a safe, comfortable place
required_materials: A cushion, blanket or soft toy
activity_description: Set up a cosy corner with a cushion and a soft toy where the child can go when upset. Stay nearby and offer comfort. Over time, they learn this is a place to feel better.
cultural_relevance: A quiet corner with a mat and a kanga works in any home.

developmental_goal: Help the child practise caring for others through pretend play
required_materials: A doll or soft toy; a small cloth for a blanket
activity_description: Give the child a doll and a small cloth and show them how to tuck the doll in, rock it and sing to it. Let them care for the doll their own way, and talk about how the doll feels.
cultural_relevance: A homemade doll wrapped in a scrap of kanga is ideal.

developmental_goal: Help the child feel part of the family at regular mealtimes
activity_description: Keep regular mealtimes and eat together as a family when you can. Let the child sit with everyone, talk about the food and the day, and keep screens away from the table.
cultural_relevance: Sharing meals together is an important tradition in many Kenyan families.

developmental_goal: Help the child understand opposites such as big and small
activity_description: Play with pairs of opposites using everyday objects and actions: a big spoon and a small spoon, walking fast then slow, talking loudly then quietly. Name the pair each time and let the child show you.
cultural_relevance: Kitchen items such as big and small sufurias make clear examples.

developmental_goal: Help the child notice what is the same and what is different
required_materials: Pairs of identical objects or pictures
activity_description: Collect pairs of matching objects, such as two spoons, two bottle tops and two socks, and mix them up. Ask the child to find the ones that are the same. Look for matching pictures in books too.
cultural_relevance: Socks from the laundry and bottle tops make an easy matching game.

developmental_goal: Help the child learn to solve problems with gentle guidance
activity_description: When the child meets a small problem, such as a lid that won't open, don't fix it straight away. Ask 'What could we try?', suggest an idea or two, and let them test it. Praise their effort whatever happens.
cultural_relevance: Everyday tasks at home offer plenty of small problems to solve.

developmental_goal: Help the child practise counting during everyday movement
activity_description: Count out loud together as you climb stairs, take steps, clap or touch fingers and toes. Start with small numbers and let the child join in. Make it part of daily routines.
cultural_relevance: Count in Kiswahili and English: moja, mbili, tatu.

developmental_goal: Help the child use their imagination to turn a box into something new
activity_description: Give the child a large cardboard box and help them turn it into a house, a car or a bus. Decorate it with crayons and talk about what it is and where it's going. Join their pretend play.
cultural_relevance: Large boxes from shops or appliances are free and endlessly useful.

activity_name: Who, What and Where Story Questions
developmental_goal: Help the child think about and answer questions about stories
required_materials: A picture book or a told story
activity_description: While reading or telling a story, ask simple questions: 'Who is this?', 'What is she doing?', 'Where did the goat go?' Give them time to answer, and help with words if needed.
cultural_relevance: Works with books or with oral stories told by grandparents.

developmental_goal: Help the child hear how words should sound
activity_description: When the child says a word incorrectly, don't correct them directly. Just repeat it back the right way in your answer: if they say 'nana', say 'Yes, a banana!' They learn by hearing the correct word.
cultural_relevance: Helpful in any language, including when children are learning two languages.

developmental_goal: Help the child learn to use longer, fuller sentences
activity_description: When the child speaks, answer with a slightly longer sentence using fuller words. If they say 'Car go', say 'Yes, the red car is going fast.' Keep it natural and warm.
cultural_relevance: Works during everyday talk at home and on outings.

developmental_goal: Help the child learn to say their first name and age
activity_description: Practise in a playful way: 'What's your name?', 'How old are you?' Show the number of years on your fingers. Praise them when they answer and keep practising at family gatherings.
cultural_relevance: Fits greetings practised with visitors and relatives.

developmental_goal: Help the child enjoy books and stories
required_materials: Books from a library, church or school
activity_description: Read together often and visit a local library or reading corner if there is one. Let the child choose books. Talk about the pictures and the story.
cultural_relevance: Community libraries, church libraries and Kenya National Library Service branches offer free books.

activity_name: Running Up to Kick a Ball
developmental_goal: Help the child practise running and kicking
activity_description: Once the child can kick a ball while standing, show them how to run up and kick it. Take turns and set up a simple goal between two stones. Cheer every kick.
cultural_relevance: A homemade ball of tied plastic bags is common for football in Kenya.

developmental_goal: Help the child start and stop moving on a signal
activity_description: Say 'Ready, set... go!' before pushing the child on a swing or before a short race. Pause before 'go' so they wait and anticipate. Play 'stop and go' by calling stop for them to freeze.
cultural_relevance: Great fun at a playground or in the compound with siblings.

developmental_goal: Build hand and finger strength for later skills like writing and buttoning
activity_description: Make playdough together and let the child squeeze, roll, pinch and poke it. Show them how to roll snakes and balls. Strong fingers help later with writing, buttoning and cutting.
cultural_relevance: Make playdough from flour, salt, water and a little oil; add food colouring if you have it.

developmental_goal: Help the child control a crayon to draw lines and circles
activity_description: Give the child crayons and paper, or chalk on a floor or wall where it's allowed. Let them scribble freely, then show them how to draw a line and a circle and let them copy.
cultural_relevance: Chalk on a cement floor or a slate is a low-cost option.

developmental_goal: Build the child's balance and strength with animal moves
activity_description: Try harder animal moves: balance on one leg like a flamingo, then crab walk with hands and feet on the floor and tummy up. Take turns and count how long you can each hold the balance.
cultural_relevance: Fun to play outdoors with friends and siblings.

developmental_goal: Help the child practise hopping and jumping
required_materials: Chalk or a stick to draw squares
activity_description: Draw a simple hopscotch with a few squares in chalk or in the soil. Show the child how to jump with two feet into each square, then try hopping on one foot. Hold their hand at first if needed.
cultural_relevance: Hopscotch is a familiar playground game in Kenya, drawn in the soil with a stick.

developmental_goal: Help the child build strength and confidence through outdoor play
required_materials: A safe park, playground or open space
activity_description: Take the child to a safe park or playground and let them run, climb low structures and explore. Stay close on climbing equipment and let them try things at their own pace.
cultural_relevance: Public parks, school fields and open compound spaces all work.

developmental_goal: Help the child explore paint with their fingers and create art
required_materials: Paint or coloured flour paste; paper
activity_description: Give the child paper and some paint, or a homemade paste of flour, water and food colouring, and let them paint with their fingers. Talk about the colours and how it feels. Display their art proudly.
cultural_relevance: Flour paste coloured with food colouring is cheap and safe.

developmental_goal: Help the child explore sand by scooping, pouring and filling
required_materials: Sand; cups, spoons and a funnel
